title: Virtual network peering
learningObjective: Create and configure regional and global VNet peering, including hub-and-spoke designs with gateway transit and forwarded traffic.
foundation: Peering connects two virtual networks so their resources talk using private IP addresses over the Microsoft backbone, as if they were one network.
Peering works within a region (regional) or across regions (global). The two address spaces must not overlap.
Peering is not transitive: if A is peered with Hub and Hub with B, A still cannot reach B on its own.
engineer: A peering is two links, one in each VNet. Status is Initiated until both exist, then Connected. The portal creates both links in one step when you have permissions on both VNets; with the CLI you create each side.

Settings per link: Allow access to the remote VNet, Allow forwarded traffic (accept traffic that an NVA in the other VNet forwards, not originated there), Allow gateway transit (on the hub: let peers use this VNet's VPN/ExpressRoute gateway), Use remote gateways (on the spoke: use the hub's gateway; the spoke must not have its own gateway).
Spoke-to-spoke traffic needs a hub NVA or Azure Firewall plus UDRs in the spokes, or Azure Virtual Network Manager connectivity configurations, or Virtual WAN.
Peering works across subscriptions and Microsoft Entra tenants (with permissions on both sides). Address spaces of peered VNets can be resized after peering, followed by a sync of the peering.
Costs: peering traffic is charged per GB for both ingress and egress; global peering charges are higher.

example.title: Shared services hub
body: Contoso runs domain controllers and a VPN gateway in vnet-hub. Each app team has a spoke peered to the hub with Use remote gateways, so spokes reach on-premises through one gateway.
Spokes are isolated from each other until the security team adds Azure Firewall in the hub and UDRs sending 10.0.0.0/8 to it.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription and a resource group (rg-net)
limits: 500 peerings per VNet (more with Azure Virtual Network Manager)
Use remote gateways requires the remote VNet to have a gateway and the local VNet to have none
portal: Enter both link names, choose the remote VNet, set allow access, forwarded traffic, gateway transit or use remote gateways.
Check Peering status is Connected on both VNets.
configuration.cli:
az network vnet peering create -g rg-net -n spoke1-to-hub --vnet-name vnet-spoke1 --remote-vnet vnet-hub --allow-vnet-access --allow-forwarded-traffic --use-remote-gateways
az network vnet peering create -g rg-net -n hub-to-spoke1 --vnet-name vnet-hub --remote-vnet vnet-spoke1 --allow-vnet-access --allow-gateway-transit
az network vnet peering list -g rg-net --vnet-name vnet-hub -o table
configuration.powershell:
$hub = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -Name vnet-hub -ResourceGroupName rg-net
$sp = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -Name vnet-spoke1 -ResourceGroupName rg-net
Add-AzVirtualNetworkPeering -Name hub-to-spoke1 -VirtualNetwork $hub -RemoteVirtualNetworkId $sp.Id -AllowGatewayTransit
Add-AzVirtualNetworkPeering -Name spoke1-to-hub -VirtualNetwork $sp -RemoteVirtualNetworkId $hub.Id -UseRemoteGateways -AllowForwardedTraffic

lab.objective: Build hub-and-spoke peering and prove it is non-transitive.
steps: Run the default spoke1 → spoke2 test and read why it fails.
Apply 'Spoke to spoke via hub NVA'.
Apply 'Overlapping address space' and 'Only one side created'.

validation.text: Connected a spoke to the hub
Routed spoke to spoke via the hub NVA

failureScenarios: Peering created on one side only
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.fix: Create the peering from the remote VNet too.
Add a hub NVA/Firewall with UDRs, or peer the spokes directly.
Hub: Allow gateway transit; spoke: Use remote gateways.

comparisons.difference: Encrypted IPsec tunnel through gateways with bandwidth limits; peering is lower latency and higher bandwidth.
Also non-transitive; AWS Transit Gateway is the hub equivalent.

misconceptions.myth: Peering is transitive through a hub.
misconceptions.reality: It is not; use an NVA, Virtual WAN or direct peerings.
Peering is billed per GB in and out.

architectureDecisions: Use hub-and-spoke with a central firewall for shared services and inspection.
Plan non-overlapping address spaces up front.
Consider Azure Virtual Network Manager for many spokes.

walkthrough.subtitle: Connect two virtual networks so they talk privately over Microsoft's backbone.

steps.label: Separate networks
steps.title: Two teams, two VNets, one app
body: The web team's VNet must reach the database team's VNet, privately and fast, without a VPN.

steps.label: Peering
steps.title: Peering joins two VNets
body: VNet peering connects two VNets so their resources talk using private IPs over the Microsoft backbone, with low latency. It works in the same region or across regions (global peering) and across subscriptions and tenants.

steps.label: Not transitive
steps.title: Peering is not transitive
body: If Spoke 1 is peered to the hub and Spoke 2 is peered to the hub, Spoke 1 still cannot reach Spoke 2. Either peer the spokes directly, or route through a firewall or NVA in the hub with user-defined routes.

callout.text: Exam favourite: A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C.

steps.label: Options
steps.title: Peering settings that matter
body: 'Allow gateway transit' on the hub plus 'Use remote gateways' on the spoke lets spokes use the hub's VPN gateway. 'Allow forwarded traffic' accepts traffic that did not start in the peered VNet, which is needed when routing through an NVA.

steps.label: Rules
steps.title: Rules of peering
body: Address spaces must not overlap. A peering has two links, one in each VNet; both must show Connected. Inbound and outbound data across peering is charged.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Peering
recap: Regional or global, cross-subscription and tenant
Gateway transit + use remote gateways to share a VPN gateway
Allow forwarded traffic for NVA routing
No overlapping ranges; both links Connected

handsOn.title: Peer two VNets and confirm both links
handsOn.cost: Free without VMs. Data across peering is charged per GB, but you send none.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

A virtual network vnet-lab (10.10.0.0/16) in rg-az104-lab with a subnet snet-app (10.10.1.0/24): Virtual networks > + Create > IP addresses tab. For these labs, untick 'Enable private subnet' on snet-app so lab VMs can reach the internet (in production use a NAT gateway instead).

steps.do: Create a second VNet in rg-az104-lab: vnet-lab2, address space 10.20.0.0/16, subnet snet-db 10.20.1.0/24.

steps.see: A form with two sections: this VNet and the remote VNet.

steps.do: Remote peering link name: lab2-to-lab; remote VNet: vnet-lab2. Local peering link name: lab-to-lab2. Leave 'Allow access' ticked on both sides. Add.
steps.see: After a moment the peering status shows Connected.
The matching link lab2-to-lab, also Connected. The portal created both directions.

steps.do: Try a third VNet with an overlapping range (10.10.0.0/16) and peer it to vnet-lab.
steps.see: Peering is refused because the address spaces overlap. Delete that VNet.

steps.do: Read the options 'Allow gateway transit' and 'Use remote gateways' on the peering.
steps.see: They are only useful when a VNet has a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway.

cleanup: Delete the peering, or: When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
